---
title: "Restrictions on the report family"
subtitle: "2.12 · postrank's report families; four-unit example after the theory book, chapter 14"
description: "Consequences of grade caps, exact grade counts and fixed-order restrictions for minimum risk."
---

An optimum is defined relative to a specified family of reports. A grade cap, an exact number of occupied grades
and contiguous cuts of a declared order impose different restrictions. The rows compare each family's minimum risk
at a common withholding cost and on a common scale. Reordering the units changes the fixed-order family, while
leaving the unrestricted family unchanged. The examples identify when a restricted optimum coincides with the
unrestricted optimum and when the restriction raises risk. Each result is accompanied by the family over which it
was obtained.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Exactly six.** The family contains 720 strict rankings. Its best report costs .0480, while the unrestricted
  reference costs .0372. Requiring every site to have its own grade forces the report to state an uncertain direction.
  The selected row identifies this direction and its error probability.
- **At most three.** The capped family contains 603 reports, including reports that use fewer grades. Exactly the
  required number gives a smaller family of 540. Here both best risks are .0417; the shared scale makes that
  equality visible. Further grade restrictions can change the minimum at this fixed cost.
- **B before A.** The declared order allows 32 contiguous reports. Its best cut costs .0379, above the unrestricted
  .0372. The unit arrows modify the declared order. The dynamic program searches cuts of the declared order, and the row checks its answer against enumeration of those same cuts.
- **Two criteria.** The four-unit example has 24 reports with every grade distinct, 75 in the unrestricted family,
  and 8 contiguous cuts. The exact-count row costs 7/40. The law's table gives the criterion-specific errors and their weighted average: the orange segment now measures expected weighted wrong directions.

- **A dominating set.** At τ = 4/9, every unrestricted best report separates {A, B} above {X, Y}, at risk 4/15.
  The best report with the grade cap costs 17/54 and puts X with A. The cap can make the separating rearrangement
  infeasible. The law panel checks the strict cross-set premise again whenever you change the price.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Every optimum belongs to a declared family. Enlarging a family cannot increase its smallest risk at a fixed
price, but changing the price changes the decision problem. The dashed mark is the all-withheld risk; an
exact-count family need not contain that report. Equal-risk reports are identified in the rows, and the order
family states its tie rule. All examples are specified for teaching.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="In postrank"}
```r
library(postrank)
sc <- postrank_expected_rank(pr_tutorial$one)
postrank_cuts(sc, pr_tutorial$one, postrank_settings(weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.2, G_max=6L, exact_G=6L), rule="optimal")$risk
```
This cuts the expected-rank order; its result agrees with the exact-count optimum here.
:::

Standalone: [families](../../embed/families.html), for example `?family=exact&G=2&tau=.40`.

Related applications: [Reporting risk and withholding cost](price-of-silence.qmd), [Grade reports as pairwise decisions](report-builder.qmd).
